name: antislop-fiction
title: Antislop (fiction register)
description: The creative-writing half of the antislop sampler, which is where almost all of its 2500 phrases and 2000 words live. Ten constructions rather than a transcription: the lists are dominated by fantasy proper nouns (Elara, Kael, Eldoria) and single verbs (nodded, whispered, flickered) that carry no signal outside the register. Do not enable this on documentation.

rules.name: “Voice barely above a whisper”
rules.description: The single most over-represented construction in the creative-writing lists. It heads both the phrase list and the trigram list.
rules.suggest: Let the line carry the volume, or say how loud they actually were.

hit: “I know,” she said, her voice barely above a whisper.
His voice was barely audible over the rain.
She answered, voice barely a whisper.
miss: He whispered the password.
The whisper carried across the hall.

rules.name: “Heart pounding in her chest”
rules.description: Interior-state telegraphing, and a redundancy: the heart is already in the chest.
rules.suggest: Cut it, or give the body something specific to do.

hit: Her heart was pounding in her chest.
His heart hammered against his ribs.
My heart skipped a beat.
miss: The drum pounded through the floor.
She pressed a hand to her chest.

rules.name: “Sent a shiver down her spine”
rules.description: The stock somatic reaction, present in four separate spellings in the shipped phrase list.
rules.suggest: Pick a reaction that belongs to this character and this moment.

hit: The sound sent a shiver down her spine.
He felt a chill run up his spine.
Shivers ran down my spine.
miss: She traced a finger along his spine.
The book's spine had cracked.

rules.name: “The sun dipped below the horizon”
rules.description: The establishing-shot sunset, usually followed by shadows being cast. Four of its fragments make the top-twenty trigrams.
rules.suggest: Say what time it is, or cut to what happens next.

hit: The sun dipped below the horizon, casting long shadows.
The sun hung low in the sky, painting the fields orange.
Streetlights came on, casting long shadows across the yard.
miss: The sun set at seven.
She dipped the brush in the water.

rules.name: “Felt like an eternity”
rules.description: Duration inflation in place of an actual duration.
rules.suggest: Give the real interval, or show what filled it.

hit: The silence felt like an eternity.
They waited for what seemed like hours.
Time stood still.
miss: The flight felt long.
It took an eternity to load, she joked.

rules.name: “The words hung in the air”
rules.description: The beat of significance dropped after a line of dialogue, so the reader knows it landed.
rules.suggest: Trust the line. If it needs help, the line is the problem.

hit: The words hung in the air between them.
The air was thick with the scent of smoke.
The room fell silent.
miss: Laundry hung in the yard.
The air smelled of rain.

rules.name: “Little did she know”
rules.description: Narrator-flagged foreshadowing, including the closer that promises a sequel.
rules.suggest: Delete it. The reader finds out anyway, and the tease costs the surprise.

hit: Little did she know what waited upstairs.
Their troubles were only just beginning.
Life would never be the same.
miss: She knew little about the protocol.
The meeting was just beginning.

rules.name: “Maybe, just maybe”
rules.description: The wistful closer. Both halves ship as separate entries in the phrase list, which is how often they co-occur.
rules.suggest: End on the last real thing that happened.

hit: Maybe, just maybe, they would make it.
It was not much, but for now, that was enough.
And maybe that was enough.
miss: Maybe we should leave.
That was enough rope to reach the branch.

rules.name: “They would face it together”
rules.description: The resolve-and-embrace ending, which resolves nothing.
rules.suggest: Let the last scene stand without a summary of how everyone felt about it.

hit: Whatever came next, they would face it together.
She was ready to face whatever the morning held.
miss: They faced each other across the table.
He was ready for the interview.

rules.name: “Something else entirely”
rules.description: Withholding as a substitute for description: the thing is named only as not-the-other-thing.
rules.suggest: Name it. If it cannot be named yet, describe what the character can actually perceive.

hit: This was something else entirely.
There was something darker behind the door.
It was unlike anything she had ever seen.
miss: We ordered something else.
The room was darker than he remembered.
